accuracy.reason: All nine objectives correctly distinguish linearizability, eventual request completion, live-node network partition and conditional impossibility. Majority behavior is explicitly scoped to an agreement protocol rather than claiming quorum counts alone guarantee safety.

evidence.quote: The required order follows completed-before-started relationships, not a globally synchronized timestamp on every request.

mechanisms.reason: The isolated reader trace derives the missing-information conflict, including blocked original write and why guessing fails. Majority/minority and conflict-reconciliation branches expose user-visible consequences; CAPDiagram faithfully illustrates them.

evidence.quote: Guessing the new value cannot guarantee correctness across possible unseen writes.

coherence.reason: Declared program/network/client prerequisites suffice; scope, partition, precise C/A definitions and impossibility precede CP/AP behavior, conditional convergence and operation-level design.

evidence.quote: Convergence means agreement on a resulting state.

decisions.reason: Explains refusal/pending versus stale responses, conflict intent loss, continued safe-majority operations and the need to evaluate latency/capacity/cost separately. Profile, reservation and edit choices transfer the guarantees to requirements.

evidence.quote: Outside partitions, CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability.

clarity.reason: Plain definitions distinguish successful operation from error reply and indefinite from bounded waiting. Compact examples teach the information barrier. Diagram and shared assets inspected without claiming rendered UI verification.

evidence.quote: An error response is not successful completion of the requested operation.

outcomes.reason: Defines distributed copies and required communication, live reachable partitioned nodes, partition tolerance and the conditional guarantee limit; rejects any-two-at-all-times and design omission as protection.

Accurately explains real-time order, overlapping operations, later-read requirement, convergence/ACID distinction, successful eventual per-request completion without latency bound, and why refusal/errors/uptime differ.

Transfers 10/12 example to 0/1, identifies B missing the completed write, analyzes stale reply and indefinite wait/refusal, and explains indistinguishability of unseen writes rather than lucky guessing.

Explains safe operations continuing on a majority while unsafe requests fail/wait; separates stale reads from divergent accepted writes and requires merge/selection/human policy without promising intent or cross-record invariants.

States quiescence, resumed communication/propagation and reconciliation conditions; rejects deadline/read-your-writes/intent guarantees. Contrasts strict and stale-tolerant operations through partition and recovery and separates configuration from vendor labels and healthy-system costs.

sourceChecks.claim: Gilbert/Lynch original PDF downloaded live after web timeout; abstract and theorem 1 establish impossibility for distributed read/write objects in partitioned executions.
PDF sections 2.2-2.3 model live responding nodes and arbitrarily lost messages; partition tolerance does not imply both guarantees.
PDF section 2.1 defines atomic/linearizable total order and completed write before later read; no global clock required. ACID and eventual meanings are distinguished.
PDF section 2.2 requires termination for every request at non-failing nodes and explicitly gives no time bound; valid operation responses, rather than service-unavailable refusal, are required.
PDF theorem 1 proof divides nodes into disjoint groups with lost messages then completes a write in one before reading the other, matching the information-barrier example.
Raft paper requires a communicating operational majority for progress and preserves committed log history via election/log protocol; two-of-three example is appropriately protocol-qualified.
Brewer explains continued partition operation, threatened invariants, explicit recovery and cases requiring manual conflict resolution; availability supplies no automatic merge.

DynamoDB documents old results under eventual reads and optional strong reads; Brewer recovery discussion supports convergence with restored communication/reconciliation and possible lost intent. No fixed delay is promised.

Brewer treats choices per operation/invariant and consistency scope, distinguishing partition decisions from ordinary operation; examples make requirement choices rather than universal product classifications.
